title: Product owner situations
authored: Project-authored reflective scenarios (2026-10-23). Not a validated situational judgment test; there are no correct answers.

scenarios.title: Mid-sprint change
scenarios.prompt: Three days into a sprint, a stakeholder asks for an urgent item to be added.

options.text: Refuse; the sprint is committed and the item goes to the next one.
Ask the team what they could swap out to make room.
Add it; urgent business needs come first.
Check how urgent it really is before deciding anything.

scenarios.title: Vague stories in refinement
scenarios.prompt: The team says several backlog items are too vague to estimate. Refinement keeps running over time.

options.text: Write fuller stories with acceptance criteria before each session.
Invite the team to write the stories with you during refinement.
Let the team start with a spike and refine the details as they learn.
Ask a business analyst to help shape the backlog.

scenarios.title: Acceptance criteria dispute
scenarios.prompt: The team says a story is done. You think one acceptance criterion is not really met, though it is arguable.

options.text: Reject the story and explain exactly what is missing.
Accept it and create a follow-up story for the gap.
Discuss it with the team and agree together what done means here.
Accept it; the disagreement is not worth the friction.

scenarios.title: Velocity drop
scenarios.prompt: The team's delivered points dropped for three sprints. Stakeholders are asking why.

options.text: Ask the team in the retrospective what is slowing them down.
Explain to stakeholders that velocity is not a productivity measure.
Analyse the sprint data yourself to find the pattern.
Leave it to the Scrum Master and engineering manager.

scenarios.title: Harsh demo feedback
scenarios.prompt: At a sprint review, a stakeholder criticises a delivered feature harshly in front of the team.

options.text: Defend the team's work and the decisions behind it on the spot.
Thank them, capture the feedback and follow up privately.
Ask clarifying questions to separate the real issues from frustration.
Accept the criticism and promise changes in the next sprint.

scenarios.title: Bug or feature
scenarios.prompt: A moderate bug affects a few users. A promised feature for many users is ready to start.

options.text: Fix the bug first; quality issues erode trust.
Start the feature; it delivers more value overall.
Apply a bug-priority policy agreed with stakeholders in advance.
Ask whether a workaround for the bug is acceptable for now.

scenarios.title: Shortcut on the definition of done
scenarios.prompt: To make a release, the team proposes skipping documentation that the definition of done requires.

options.text: Hold the line; the definition of done exists for moments like this.
Allow it once, with a story to finish the documentation next sprint.
Allow it; documentation can follow when there is time.
Write the essential documentation yourself so the release can go.

scenarios.title: Splitting a large epic
scenarios.prompt: An epic is too large for one release. The team proposes splitting by technical layer; you would rather split by user value.

options.text: Insist on value slices and explain why releases should be usable.
Go with the team's split; they understand the technical risks.
Run a story-mapping session to find a split everyone accepts.
Combine both: a thin technical foundation, then value slices.

scenarios.title: Availability to the team
scenarios.prompt: Stakeholder meetings take most of your week, and developers say they cannot reach you with questions.

options.text: Hold a fixed daily office hour for the team.
Delegate day-to-day decisions to a senior developer within clear limits.
Answer questions asynchronously in the team channel whenever you can.
Cut back stakeholder meetings so the team comes first.

scenarios.title: Two managers, two priorities
scenarios.prompt: Two senior managers give you conflicting priorities for the same quarter.

options.text: Get them in one room and ask them to agree a single order.
Decide based on product goals and inform both of the reasoning.
Serve both partially so neither is blocked.
Escalate to the person both managers report to.

scenarios.title: Refinement runs long
scenarios.prompt: A refinement meeting has run 40 minutes over. The team is discussing implementation details of one story.

options.text: Stop the discussion and move the details to a separate session.
Let it run; the discussion seems valuable.
Ask the team whether to continue or park it.
Time-box the remaining discussion to ten minutes.

scenarios.title: Release communication
scenarios.prompt: A release includes a change that will surprise some users, though it is an improvement overall.

options.text: Announce it clearly in advance, including what users lose.
Ship it with release notes and handle feedback as it comes.
Highlight the benefits and keep the downsides brief.
Contact the most affected users personally before release.
